title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: The ₹100 Unit-Economics Machine—and Its Hidden Lease Drag

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, margin is sanity, but cash conversion after rent and capex is reality.
epigraph.author: Institutional Retail Maxim

web_blocks.html: Distribution is only half the retail battle. The real moat sits in how much of every ₹100 survives COGS, store rent, and capex. Lenskart pairs company-owned (COCO) metro flagships with capital-light franchise (FOFO) outlets in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns [3][12]. Franchise partners fund store fit-outs, while Lenskart supplies centralized inventory, cloud POS, and brand pull.

Centralized automated manufacturing powers that retail network. The Bhiwadi plant uses Addverb robotics for lens surfacing, coating, edging, and inspection [8]. Designing private-label frames and grinding lenses in-house cuts out three distributor layers. Q4 FY26 gross margin reached 69.6%, leaving nearly ₹70 per ₹100 of sales to cover stores, staff, and overhead [10][12].

web_blocks.caption: FY2026 Consolidated ₹100 Revenue-to-FCF Waterfall (Audited Statutory Basis, ₹ Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of ₹8,814 Cr in FY26 revenue, ₹7,060 Cr (80.1%) is absorbed by operating expenses, yielding ₹1,754 Cr in statutory Ind AS 116 operating profit (19.9% OPM). After ₹1,048 Cr D&A (heavily inflated by Ind AS 116 Right-of-Use store lease amortization), ₹178 Cr interest, ₹153 Cr other income, and ₹179 Cr tax, Net Profit is ₹501 Cr (5.68% margin). Statutory CFO of ₹1,670 Cr less ₹824 Cr capex produces ₹846 Cr Free Cash Flow—though investors must adjust for lease principal outflows sitting in financing cash flows.

web_blocks.html: A unit-economics audit must separate store-level payback from corporate cash flow. In India, mature stores report 33%+ store-level EBITDA margins and ~10-month capex payback [12]. That fast payback funded 603 net new stores in FY26 (542 India, 61 international) [3][12]. At the corporate level, two wedges compress that 33% store margin:

web_blocks.takeaway: Lenskart's four-wall store economics are genuinely attractive, but statutory Ind AS 116 EBITDA (19.9%) overstates cash operating profitability by ~800 bps relative to true pre-rent EBITDA (~11.5% consolidated; 14.3% India, 7.0% International).

web_blocks.html: Supply-chain resilience is a key bear watchpoint. Bhiwadi and the planned ₹1,500 crore Hyderabad plant localize lens grinding, yet Lenskart still imports raw frames and acetate from China [7][11]. Any tariff hike or import curb could squeeze that 69.6% gross margin. In addition, central-lab synchronization carries execution risk: if Hyderabad commissioning slips, delivery times lengthen and unit overhead rises [11].

web_blocks.mechanism: Scaled a vertically integrated D2C-plus-retail model combining ~300 physical 'SmileShops' with centralized 3D-printed aligner manufacturing, relying on heavy marketing spend and consumer financing to drive top-line growth.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Peaked at ~$750M revenue and ~300 shops in 2019; revenue fell ~37% by 2022 with an $86.4M net loss; filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Sept 2023 with ~$890.6M–$900M in funded debt and >$1B liabilities before full liquidation in Dec 2023 [13].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Centralized manufacturing plus physical retail 'try-on' shops only compounds if organic repeat purchase (Lenskart Gold) replaces paid CAC and store leases stay self-funded; if SSSG stalls under high fixed lab and lease obligations, operating leverage reverses violently.

web_blocks.html: Look closely at the store-expansion engine behind that ₹100 waterfall. In India, Lenskart mixes company-owned (COCO) metro flagships with franchise-owned (FOFO) outlets in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns [3][12]. Franchisees fund local store fit-outs, while Lenskart controls inventory, cloud POS software, and brand marketing. Because central labs in Bhiwadi (and soon Hyderabad) hold prescription-lens stock, stores need minimal back-room inventory [7][8]. That hub-and-spoke design keeps Debtor Days at 7 days and compresses the Cash Conversion Cycle to 19 days in FY26 [1]. Mature Indian stores pay back capex in roughly 10 months [12].

Notice also how vertical integration protects gross margins during promotional cycles. Even with Gold Buy-One-Get-One offers, Q4 FY26 gross margin held at 69.6% [10][12]. Why? Because private-label frames and in-house lens surfacing keep landed product cost near ₹30.40 per ₹100 of sales [10]. The upcoming ₹1,500 crore Hyderabad mega-facility at Tukkuguda will expand capacity for South India and international exports [7]. Once ramped, lower logistics distances should further support pre-Ind AS store margins.

book_paragraphs: Whenever a consumer brand tells you it has 'disrupted' a traditional industry, the first thing you and I should ask is simple: show me what happens to ₹100 at the cash register. In Lenskart's case, that ₹100 waterfall tells a story of extraordinary industrial efficiency at the top of the income statement, followed by a surprisingly heavy toll from store leases and factory depreciation on the way down.

Start at the top. In FY26, Lenskart generated ₹8,814 crore in consolidated sales. Because it designs its own frames—like Vincent Chase and John Jacobs—and grinds its own lenses inside robotic facilities in Bhiwadi, its cost of materials is roughly ₹30.40 out of every ₹100. That leaves nearly ₹70 of gross profit—far richer than a typical multi-brand retailer that has to share margin with wholesalers and luxury licensors.

Now watch what happens next. Employee costs—optometrists in 3,300+ stores, factory engineers, and tech teams—consume about ₹22.90 per ₹100, and other operating expenses like marketing, freight, and utilities take another ₹26.80. On a statutory basis, that leaves ₹19.90 of operating profit (₹1,754 crore). Look closer, though, and you spot the Ind AS 116 accounting quirk: because Lenskart capitalizes its store leases onto the balance sheet, roughly ₹720 crore to ₹750 crore of actual cash rent disappears from operating expenses and reappears below the line as depreciation (₹11.89 per ₹100) and lease interest (₹2.02 per ₹100).

Taken together, Lenskart's distribution and manufacturing engine explains why it can absorb heavy store expansion and still generate ₹846 Cr in annual free cash flow. Every ₹100 of FY26 revenue leaves nearly ₹70 in gross profit, ₹18.95 in operating cash flow, and ₹9.60 in free cash flow after capex—a rare financial signature in physical retail.

book_subsections.title: Four-Wall Payback vs. Corporate Cash Conversion
paragraphs: When you strip out that lease accounting distortion, Lenskart's true pre-Ind AS EBITDA margin in FY26 was roughly 14.3% in India and 7.0% internationally—around ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,032 crore consolidated. That is still a healthy inflection from single-digit margins just two years prior, and it is anchored by rapid store-level economics: mature Indian stores generate over 33% four-wall EBITDA and pay back their initial fit-out capex in roughly ten months.

Yet history offers a sobering warning about vertically integrated D2C-to-retail hybrids. Consider SmileDirectClub in the United States, which paired central automated manufacturing with roughly 300 physical 'SmileShops' and peaked at $750 million in revenue in 2019. When customer acquisition costs surged and regulatory friction hit, its fixed lab and lease commitments crushed cash flow, ending in Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023 with $900 million in debt. Lenskart's critical defense against that fate is organic repeat frequency: unlike one-off teeth aligners, myopia requires lifetime replacement, and Lenskart's Gold membership keeps customers returning without paying Google or Meta a second time.

book_subsections.title: Inside the ₹100 Revenue Waterfall and Bhiwadi's Automated Edge
paragraphs: Why can Lenskart earn a nearly 70% gross margin while selling prescription glasses at half the price of traditional luxury opticians? The answer sits in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, and in the planned ₹1,500 Cr mega-factory in Tukkuguda, Hyderabad. Traditional Indian opticians buy frames from wholesale distributors and outsource lens grinding to fragmented local labs, layering three to four distributor markups onto the final bill. Lenskart eliminated every middleman: it designs frames in-house, manufactures and edges lenses using automated German robotics in Bhiwadi, and ships finished spectacles directly to stores or doorsteps within 24 to 72 hours.

Let's trace every ₹100 of Lenskart's FY26 consolidated revenue (₹8,814 Cr) down to free cash flow. Out of every ₹100 collected at the register or app checkout, roughly ₹30 to ₹31 goes to raw materials and cost of goods sold, leaving nearly ₹70 in gross profit. Employee benefits—including in-store optometrists and factory technicians—and other operating expenses (marketing, logistics, and non-lease overheads) consume about ₹49, leaving ₹19.90 in statutory Ind AS 116 operating profit.

From that ₹19.90, non-cash depreciation and amortization takes ₹11.90 (reflecting both factory machinery and capitalized right-of-use store leases), interest costs take ₹2.00, other income adds ₹1.70, and taxes take ₹2.00—leaving ₹5.70 in statutory net profit. Yet when you look at the cash flow statement, adding back non-cash depreciation and working-capital discipline produces ₹18.95 in operating cash flow per ₹100 of revenue (₹1,670 Cr total). After deducting ₹9.35 in capital expenditures (₹824 Cr for new stores and manufacturing capacity), Lenskart generated ₹9.60 in unlevered free cash flow per ₹100 of sales (₹846 Cr) in FY26.

book_subsections.title: Franchisee vs. Company-Owned Economics & Supply-Chain Velocity
paragraphs: How does Lenskart fund 500 to 600 net new store openings a year without blowing up its balance sheet? By pairing company-owned, company-operated (COCO) flagship stores in high-footfall metros with franchise-owned, franchise-operated (FOFO) outlets in Tier-2 and Tier-3 towns. In a FOFO store, the local franchise partner puts up the store fit-out capital and carries local operating responsibility, while Lenskart supplies the centralized inventory, cloud POS software, omnichannel fulfillment, and brand marketing.

Because frames and edged lenses sit in centralized automated hubs rather than bloated back-rooms at every store, Lenskart keeps store-level working capital lean and turns inventory far faster than traditional opticians. The upcoming ₹1,500 Cr Hyderabad mega-facility at Tukkuguda is designed to push that supply-chain velocity even further—cutting delivery times across South India and serving as an export hub for Southeast Asia and the Middle East as store count scales past 3,500.

book_subsections.title: Working Capital Discipline in an Omnichannel Model
paragraphs: Many physical retail chains stumble because store expansion traps cash in slow-moving inventory and bloated receivables. Lenskart's omnichannel architecture avoids most of that friction: retail customers pay upfront at the store register or online checkout, keeping trade receivables minimal, while centralized lens edging in Bhiwadi means individual stores only hold display frames rather than deep prescription-lens stock.

That discipline shows up directly in FY26 cash conversion: ₹1,670 Cr of operating cash flow on ₹1,754 Cr of statutory operating profit—a 95% EBITDA-to-CFO conversion ratio even during a 603-store expansion year.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Respect the Rent Bill
book_callouts.text: Never let Ind AS 116 fool you into thinking a physical retailer is asset-light. Yes, Lenskart's Bhiwadi robots and 10-month store paybacks are real competitive weapons. At the same time, ₹824 crore of annual capex—plus the ₹1,500 crore Hyderabad mega-plant commitment—means cash conversion depends heavily on keeping same-store sales growing above 20%. In Chapter 4, we will test whether Lenskart's moat is wide enough to protect that store throughput against domestic and global rivals.
